key_points.point: Our DEG-based Cox regression approach for identifying prognostic gene signatures aligns with established methodologies in cancer prognosis research, as similar workflows combining differential expression analysis with survival modeling have successfully identified prognostic biomarkers across multiple cancer types including glioblastoma and laryngeal cancer.

The identification of genes with diverse hazard ratios—including both risk-associated and protective factors—reflects the biological complexity of cancer prognosis, consistent with multi-gene signature studies that demonstrate heterogeneous prognostic effects rather than uniform directional associations.

Integration of transcriptomic profiling with survival analysis to construct prognostic models represents a validated strategy for biomarker discovery, with demonstrated clinical utility in predicting patient outcomes and informing treatment decisions across various malignancies.

Our DEG-based Cox regression approach aligns with established methodologies for prognostic signature development in cancer, as similar workflows using LASSO-based feature selection have successfully identified prognostic biomarkers in glioblastoma and other malignancies.

The identification of genes with diverse hazard ratios (both risk and protective) is consistent with the heterogeneous nature of cancer biology, where integrated analysis of bulk RNA-seq data has revealed complex prognostic signatures reflecting varied cellular functions and genetic contributions to disease progression.

Our prognostic gene signature approach contributes to the growing body of work developing molecular biomarker panels for cancer prognosis, extending beyond traditional single-marker studies to capture the multifactorial nature of disease outcomes through multi-gene risk models.

Our DEG-based Cox regression workflow aligns with established methodologies for identifying prognostic gene signatures in cancer, as demonstrated by similar approaches in glioblastoma, laryngeal cancer, and gastric cancer studies that successfully identified 4-5 gene prognostic models using LASSO regression and Cox analysis.

The identification of genes with diverse hazard ratios (both risk and protective) is consistent with the heterogeneous nature of cancer prognosis, where immune-related and functional genes can exhibit opposing prognostic effects, as observed in studies identifying mixed protective and risk markers through differential expression and immune profiling.

The use of differential expression analysis combined with survival modeling represents a validated strategy for biomarker discovery, with multiple studies demonstrating that integrating transcriptomic data with clinical outcomes can successfully identify clinically relevant prognostic signatures across various cancer types.

LASSO-based feature selection represents an established computational approach for identifying prognostic biomarkers in cancer genomics, with prior applications in glioblastoma demonstrating the utility of regularized regression methods for gene signature development from TCGA datasets.

Cox regression-based workflows for prognostic gene identification are widely adopted in cancer research, enabling the derivation of multi-gene signatures with mixed hazard profiles that reflect the biological heterogeneity of tumor progression and patient outcomes.
